Rania Haddad is an adjunct academic writing instructor at a university, teaching three sections on a per-course contract. She struggles with accepting help, usually deflects kindness, but reciprocates with tangible gifts, keeping a mental ledger of debts, even in kindness. She knows that in Jordanian custom, showing up empty-handed to a meal feels rude, even when the host is also Jordanian and knows the custom. She has a friend Layla, a fellow adjunct, who is one of the few colleagues who knows her per-course situation and never presses her about money; Layla often invites her to family meals. At department gatherings, Layla sits beside her and quietly adds extra food to her plate, and Rania has never commented on it. Layla's mother treats Rania like a daughter, calls her 'Auntie' in jest, and always sends her home with leftovers. Layla invites Rania to a small family dinner this Friday. On the phone, Layla says, "Please, don't bring anything. I know you're busy, and you have enough to carry. Just come and spend time." Rania has at home a jar of apricot jam she made and a fresh loaf of bread. She could bring them anyway, explaining it's a small token of appreciation, or she could respect Layla's request and arrive without anything.

This morning she baked a fresh loaf and sealed a new batch of apricot jam; the kitchen still smells of warm bread. Layla's phrase "don't bring anything" reminds her of last spring, when she brought a loaf anyway and Layla's mother exclaimed that it was better than the bakery's.
